extracted.intended_audience: college and university mathematics instructors (those assigning and grading undergraduate math assessments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rubrics for designing, administering, and grading undergraduate mathematics assessment tasks (student-created problems, content-based interviews, expository writing, and modeling projects). Focuses on practical checklists, interview schedules, analytic and holistic scoring scales and task-management practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: No late problems policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a policy that no problems are accepted late, lest you find yourself cornered at the end of the semester with more evaluation to do than you can handle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a hard deadline for student-created problems to avoid excessive end-of-term grading load. Enforce consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare topics and determine number of problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare in advance the topics you want the students to explore. Determine the number of problems you will collect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide thematic coverage and workload up-front so students know boundaries and instructors can plan grading logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain purpose and use of student-created problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain to students the purpose of the problems and how the questions will be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell students whether problems will be used for study guides, tests, examples in class, or final exam items; clarity reduces confusion and frames student effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate desired problems and grading expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate what you want students to do. Give examples of problems in each of the grading categories for the students to use as guidelines. Involve the class in a discussion of the grade each example should receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model exemplar problems and discuss grading rationale publicly to calibrate student expectations and reduce disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give ample time to create problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Give students ample time to create a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow sufficient work time so students can produce thoughtful problems rather than rushed submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide timely feedback and return problems with comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide feedback in a timely fashion. Grade and return the problems so that they can be corrected and used. Even if you have insufficient time to organize the problems completely, return the papers with comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick turnaround enables students to use the problems as study tools; returning papers with comments is preferable to no feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make use of student problems in instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Make use of the problems, as a study guide for an upcoming test, as test questions, as examples in class, or as problems on the final examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate student-created problems into subsequent instruction and assessment to validate the exercise and reinforce learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and compliment student work
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliment the students on their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive reinforcement encourages student engagement and future quality submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer electronic submission for ease of compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, have students submit problems electronically, on disk or by e-mail. (This may not be possible with all problems.) Those not in this form can be photocopied for distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic submissions simplify organizing, collating, and editing; plan for accommodations if not all problems can be electronic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify interview goals before scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying the goal(s) of the interview. Before beginning to construct an interview schedule, the interviewer needs to clarify his or her goals for the interview (e.g., describe the interviewee's concept image of derivative, determine connections among limit/derivative/integral, determine depth of knowledge of a set of concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear goals determine the focus and structure of interview questions and follow-ups; do not use interviews primarily for grading if the aim is to understand thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design an interview schedule with core and follow-up items
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing an interview schedule of questions to be asked: include a core set of questions/tasks to be posed to every interviewee and a set of potential follow-up questions or tasks whose use depends on responses. Include directions for follow-up and plans for different circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare directions for how to proceed if the interviewee gets stuck, asks for help, or raises related points; attach copies of core questions/problems in large enough type for interviewer, interviewee, and video camera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot and revise interview schedules
rubrics_metrics.description: Piloting and revising the interview schedule. Pilot interviews (taping recommended) and revise based on whether questions are understood, are catalytic, follow-ups are useful, sequence appropriate, and camera focus decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pilot tape review and explicit checklist questions: Were questions understood as intended? Were they adequate catalysts? Were follow-ups useful? Was sequence appropriate? Decide camera focus (student work, device display, or student).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare interview logistics and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing for and conducting the interviews: prepare an 'interview box' containing schedule, tapes, batteries, folders, pen, blank/graph paper, straightedge, calculator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have supplies ready so interviewer can focus on the interaction rather than logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct interviews as probing, open-ended conversations (not tutoring or oral exams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conducting the interviews: use loosely structured questions as catalysts; probe rationale regardless of correctness; encourage open talk; probe personal phrasing and request alternate explanations; ask for instances of generalizations; continue probing when further information is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to uncover students' personal understandings and the reasons they find them reasonable; avoid teaching or turning the session into an oral exam; if you think you understand, probe further because students may surprise you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze interview data focusing on sense-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing the results: watch tapes (preferably with a colleague) to see what students write and enter and continually ask 'How does this student make sense of the mathematics he or she is using?' rather than 'Is the answer right or wrong?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use videotape evidence to link verbalizations and written/computer work; collaborative viewing aids interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interviews to diagnose misconceptions and inform instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of Findings: Interviews can reveal aspects of understanding not visible via other methods; instructors can use findings to craft examples that pose cognitive conflicts and focus discussion on distinctions (e.g., limit as process vs. limit as a number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply findings to design classroom activities and language that address robust misconceptions; accept that discussion alone may not move some students beyond procedural understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success factors for interviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Key to success: a belief that each student's understanding is unique and best revealed through open-ended questions; belief that students construct their own knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain interviewer stance as elicitor of thinking; remember interviews are not tutoring, not oral exams, and usually not teaching experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview schedule component: 'Describe or Define' (tangent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask students to define 'tangent' in their own words; ask them to explain what they mean by tangent (e.g., slope at a point) and to sketch pictures; show graphs and ask which lines are tangents and what the tangent tells about the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe student concept images and graphical interpretation; test ability to move between verbal and pictorial descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview schedule component: 'Role of tangent in calculus'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask how dropping the concept of tangent would affect the study of Calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elicits students' sense of the conceptual role and centrality of tangents in calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview schedule component: 'Symbolic representation of tangent'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask how to find a tangent given a function rule; ask about different methods and about one-sided limits (e.g., tangent at x = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe understanding of symbolic/analytic methods (derivative, limits) and one-sided behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview schedule component: 'Graphical representation of tangent'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask students to explain 'tangent' using a graph and discuss tangents for given functions (e.g., f(x)=1/x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine ability to interpret tangency in graphical contexts, including discontinuities and asymptotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview schedule component: 'Connections among slope, tangent, asymptote'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether asymptote and slope are related; whether asymptote and tangent are related, and request explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students' ability to relate multiple representational concepts and articulate connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify assignment purpose and audience for expository writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before designing writing assignments, decide why assign writing (improve exposition, introduce new math, strengthen understanding, provide feedback) and determine the intended audience (instructor, future employer, public, peer, self).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain purpose and audience to students to reduce confusion and improve alignment of writing with goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify assignment details explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Pin down specifics: word-processed vs handwritten; reasonable length; quality of writing expected; mathematical detail required; show steps vs overview; group work policy; time allowed; late policy; percentage of grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit administrative details matter to students—specify them to reduce misunderstandings and grading disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide model/example papers
rubrics_metrics.description: For short papers, provide an example of the type of writing expected (copy excellent student papers; keep on reserve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples help students understand expectations; consider using anonymized past work as exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric checklist for expository mathematics (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a checklist (rubric) with yes/no items that serves as both teaching and assessment tool; give students the checklist before assignment and require it be attached to submitted paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the checklist to make feedback concise (mark yes/no and brief comments), make grading more objective, and let the number of 'yes' responses determine the grade if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: restate the problem clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper clearly (re)state the problem to be solved?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear problem statement or restatement shows the student understands the task; mark yes/no and comment if unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: answer stated in a complete sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper state the answer in a complete sentence which stands on its own?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require an explicit final answer statement so readers can find the conclusion without parsing the entire exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: state assumptions underlying formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper clearly state the assumptions which underlie the formulas?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make students articulate modeling/derivation assumptions so solutions are interpretable and limitations are explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: provide an approach paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper provide a paragraph which explains how the problem will be approached?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A roadmap paragraph helps readers follow the mathematical development and demonstrates planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: clearly label visual representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper clearly label diagrams, tables, graphs, or other visual representations of the math (if these are indeed used)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-labeled visuals reduce ambiguity; require labels/units/axes where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: define all variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper define all variables used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids confusion and makes reasoning self-contained; mark missing definitions and ask for clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: explain derivation or cite formula sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper explain how each formula is derived, or where it can be found?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages understanding of formulas rather than blind application; cite references if formula not derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: provide acknowledgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper give acknowledgment where it is due?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require citation of sources and collaborators; teach academic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: correct spelling, grammar, punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: In this paper, are the spelling, grammar, and punctuation correct?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics matter; mark errors but avoid over-emphasis if the pedagogical goal is mathematical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: mathematical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: In this paper, is the mathematics correct?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a core criterion; distinguish between minor arithmetic slips and conceptual errors in feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist item: solution addresses original question
rubrics_metrics.description: In this paper, did the writer solve the question that was originally asked?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the student answered the posed question rather than an easier/related variant; penalize irrelevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use checklist as front-page feedback and grade
rubrics_metrics.description: Students get a copy of the checklist before their first assignment and must attach it to the front page; instructor marks yes/no and the total number of yes's is the grade on the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice teaches students expectations, streamlines grading, makes feedback transparent, and reduces grade disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid heavy instructor-driven rewrites; use audio commentary alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: If students rewrite, consider asking for an audio cassette of instructor commentary along with draft rather than heavy written editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audio comments allow richer feedback, reduce instructor editing workload, and often yield substantially improved final drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mini-deadlines for long-term projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Mandate mini-deadlines for subtasks (thesis topic, partial bibliography, list of mathematicians for searches, vocabulary list, rough draft of intro, outline with revised bibliography, rough draft, final paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staged deadlines reduce procrastination, reduce anxiety, and make supervision feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide campus resources for struggling writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure resources exist (tutors, writing center, books/articles) to help anxious or weak students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct students to supports; don't rely solely on the instructor for remedial writing help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute assessment scales at course start and discuss expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide each student with a copy of the assessment scales the first class meeting; briefly discuss and point out that numeric solution without other components will result in failing grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early exposure to the rubric aligns student work with instructor expectations and reduces misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic scale dimension: Understanding (0–3 pts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding — 3 pts: complete understanding demonstrated in problem statement, plan, and interpretation; 2 pts: good understanding with minor overlooks; 1 pt: minimal understanding; 0 pt: no understanding or missing problem statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score to reflect depth and completeness of the student's grasp; use comments to indicate specific gaps (e.g., overlooked constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic scale dimension: Plan (0–3 pts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan — 3 pts: plan clearly articulated AND will lead to a correct solution; 2 pts: reasonably articulated and correct OR has minor flaw; 1 pt: not clearly presented OR only partially correct; 0 pt: no plan or completely incorrect plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity and viability of the planned approach separately from execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic scale dimension: Solution (0–3 pts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solution — 3 pts: solution correct AND clearly labeled OR incorrect but the expected outcome of a slightly flawed plan implemented correctly; 2 pts: incorrect due to minor implementation error OR not clearly labeled; 1 pt: incorrect due to significant implementation error; 0 pt: no solution is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate conceptual plan from arithmetic/implementation errors; give credit when appropriate for correct methods with small mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic scale dimension: Presentation (0–1 pt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation — 1 pt: overall appearance neat and easy to read with pertinent information readily found; 0 pt: paper is hard to read or pertinent information hard to find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation is a binary (in this scale) criterion—neatness and navigability matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic scoring scale (4-point exemplar start)
rubrics_metrics.description: Holistic scale: 4 Points — Exemplary Response: All of the following characteristics must be present: the answer is correct; the explanation is clear and complete; the explanation includes complete implementation of a mathematically correct plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holistic scales are quicker to apply; include letter codes (e.g., 'a') to indicate which criterion is lacking when giving a composite score. Start with 4 points and increase levels only as you gain experience; be cautious: more points => harder to define reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require team contribution logs for group projects
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid freeloading, have group members log hours spent; warn that if one student logs minimal time relative to others, that person will receive a proportionally reduced share of the grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logged hours to adjust individual grades within group submissions; communicate policy and consequences clearly in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analytic scoring to give section-specific feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the analytic scale, record a separate score for each section (understanding, plan, solution, presentation) so students see specific strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This granularity provides diagnostic feedback and helps students improve targeted skills for future reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic scale practice: include advisory letter for shortcomings
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the holistic scale include a letter (e.g., '3a') to indicate which criterion was lacking to provide students guidance on shortcomings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines the efficiency of holistic scoring with some targeted feedback on weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about scale granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: As the number of points on a scale increases so does the difficulty in developing and applying the scale; begin with about four points and increase only after gaining experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scoring levels to be discriminable and reliable given instructor time and expertise.
